questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I liked the modules offered at Goldsmiths, wanted to practice my english and wanted to live and study in London, because it is one of the most exciting cities in the world :).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall it was a wonderful experience! I would say the only drawbacks were 1) the cost of living in London and 2) administrative chaos at Goldsmiths.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Things like housing and info on social activities were quite easy to find, but everything related to more practical info on choosing modules, finding my timetable etc. was a complete chaos. There had just been a "restructure", which meant that they had fired most of the administrative staff and pooled all the positions together in weird teams. The result was that no one was really able to answer any questions about modules etc., because no one believed it was part of an area they should cover. Everyone, and especially the study abroad students were confused about how to get info; the student hubs had hour-long queues and no one answered their emails due to "the number of emails they received". Hence, I didn't get my timetable until around a month after I arrived and was very confused about whether or not I had been accepted to the modules I had applied to, It worked out alright, it was just a really frustrating experience.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Technically there was assistance available from the study abroad team, but they were so busy with all the chaos in the first couple of weeks that you couldn't realistically get an answer. The lecturers were nice and tried to help, but they were also confused and frustrated with the administration, because everything had been restructured. 
Other things were easier to get info on, for example they provided assistance with things like the possibility to sign up with a GP, a campus tour etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: You could apply to stay in Loring Hall, which is on campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: In LH you share a kitchen with the other people in your flat and can cook there. No meal plans are available.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
It was not as bad as I expected :) They put all the exchange students in the same two blocks, which made it easy to socialise, and I ended up spending a lot of time with the other exchange students in my flat & building. It is quite expensive for what it is, but so is everything in London, and compared to the private rent market staying in Loring is a very low effort option. If you are not a fan of loud parties every weekend, it is a good idea to request a "quiet" flat when you apply for accommodation. I did, and it meant that the people I stayed with were a lot more calm and clean than in the "loud" building, haha. 
I'd say that the main drawback of staying there is that you have to check in any guests and they are quite strict on this. So bringing more than one visitor to your flat at a time is not really an option. And if someone comes to visit, they can only stay for up to three nights in your room.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As described above, the whole signing up for modules thing was very chaotic. Moreover, the administration sent confused emails about having to apply for visas, although you do not need a visa to visit the UK from EU if you are there for less than six months. Apart from all this confusing, I would say Goldsmiths is generally a lot better at providing info on modules etc. on their website, info on who to talk to when you are confused etc. It was just that the queues were so long that it took forever to get an answer.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: In terms of modules, we were supposed to say which modules we wanted before arriving. This form was however full of errors, where most of the modules they had listed weren't available in the term I was there. It took weeks for them to figure this out, and then we had to fill out a new form. Despite this, I was still approved for a module that wasn't offered. I ended up just emailing the study abroad department during the first two weeks of term, where you still have the possibility to change modules. This was fine for me, since none of the modules were full, but it was quite complicated for some of the other exchange students.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could talk to the student hub and email the study abroad department, and they would try to help you.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got 2 out of the 4 courses I wanted, and 2 I had not applied for initially.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have patience. Don't panic if it takes them awhile to make your timetable, just show up to the classes you expect to take anyway. Use the 2 week period you have for changing modules to go to different lectures. It is okay to not like a module you initially signed up for and wish to follow another one.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really liked Goldsmiths more critical/progressive approach and it was fun to have a semester where you mostly study theoretical/thematic modules, which I find a bit more chill than many methods modules. I was surprised at the rather more historical perspective at Goldsmiths - it is rare to study events from the 16/1700 at KU, but we did so in a couple of modules at Goldsmiths.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was fine, I think the teaching was a bit different from KU, but the level wasn't necessarily higher. Their reading lists are a bit different, but reading the key readings for each lecture was doable. Then you could look at the rest when writing essays etc.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was structured a bit differently: they have a weekly 1 hour lecture followed by a 1 hour seminar for each module. So 8 hours of teaching per week, but half of it is seminars. It was nice to experience this more classroom centered teaching, although I thought the students were very quiet in most of the seminars, at least compared to Danish high school classrooms. In general, it seemed like they didn't have much experience with oral participation; we had to do a debate in one seminar and two presentations for another module, and it seemed like quite a big thing, although I found it pretty chill. I was surprised by the emphasis they put on office hours, because we don't use it much at KU. They often encouraged us to go to the office hours to discuss our essays etc., and I think that was really nice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Confronting the climate crisis
Race, racism and social theory
Social change and political action
Visual explorations of the social world

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Race, racism and social theory was really good and covered things that are not as easy to find courses on at KU. Even though it dealt with difficult themes, it was a really sympathetically taught module and I learned a lot from it.
Visual explorations of the social world was also really nice, and fun because you got to do your own project and thus examine something you find interesting. Socially it was also quite nice to take this module, because there was a lot of workshops with group work etc. where you could get to know the other students a bit better. It was also one of very few methods modules, so good to take if you want to try that as well.
The other two were also fine, although Social change was a little simple, probably because it was a second year module. I would advise to only choose third year modules if you have the possibility, as these are way more interesting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I spent more money on tranport than I expected. This was due to going on a few weekend trips and also there was a lot of transport issues because train and bus drivers were striking all the time. I thus rented a bike to travel more freely, but still ended up using the tube and overground quite a lot when going further away etc.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Did not have to buy any books for the modules, so that was cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Loads of different things! Go to the welcome fest in the beginning of the term and see what it's possible to join. I joined the athletics team and the arts and crafts society, and that was fun. My friend really liked pole dancing, but I'm sure most of it is nice!
I also joined a critical philosophy reading group, so i would just recommend keeping an eye out for anything you are interested in, they probably have an activity related to it :)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Depends on your interests, they offer all sorts of stuff! If you stay in halls, then also try to go to some of the Loring Hall meet up things or trips if you fancy getting to know the other LH-students. And go to some of the events at the student union like the parties, trashy tuesdays, jazz evenings etc.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go on a few trips. I went to Oxford and Cambridge, which was fun. Also went to Charleston in Lewes, which is a pretty museum house about the bloomsbury group. Also try to check out some of the festivals and events happening in London or see if there is a concert you like etc. Most of the museums are free to visit, so maybe check out some of those. I also really liked to explore the areas around Goldsmiths like Peckham, Deptford, Greenwich.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Pretty easy, british culture is not that different, and London is so diverse that pretty much everyone is welcomed.
If you do feel homesick or just want to speak a bit of Danish, maybe check out the sunday dinners or events at Dansk KFUK in Hampstead, where there are loads of Danes willing to chat, give advice etc.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I think joining a sport or another kind of society is one of the easiest way to socialise. Also try to chat to the people in your modules, people are generally very welcoming.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Maybe British food being so bland, haha. No but on a personal level I don't think there is that much cultural difference between danes and brits. It was more political/societal things I found challenging, mostly because there were so so many strikes while I was there: train & bus strikes, royal mail strikes, uni strikes, nurses and ambulance strikes, which of course made daily life a little more difficult.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That most people in London are a lot more welcoming and easy going than in Denmark, and also the diversity and possibilities of London.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Try to have a flexible budget, because London is expensive. Try to save on things like food and transport rather than experiences.
Make a list of what you most want to see/do in London, because once you get there you will have so many choices that it can be hard to prioritise. 
Enjoy your modules and the possibility of "just" being a student without also working part time, volunteering etc.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try to do some work on your essays during the term, so you don't have to starte from scratch in January. Talk to your lecturers in their office hours or email them if you are confused or just want to go over an idea with them.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friendships made, everything I was able to explore in London and what I learned in the modules.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Confusion related to administrative and practical things.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
